conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: TradingRangeContext
candidates.quote: The broadest and most useful definition of a trading range is that it is simply an area of two-sided trading. It can be as small as a single bar (a doji bar) or larger than all of the bars on your screen.
candidates.description: The market is in a trading range: an area of two-sided (both-directions) trading, as opposed to trending. Shared primitive that most of this chapter's candidates depend on; the exact operational test is a design decision (bar overlap, swing-count, MA flatness, absence of sustained new highs/lows are all offered as clues in this chapter).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (regime classification underlying most range-specific entries)

complexity.reason: "the market is in a trading range" is the MINING.md canonical research example: the concept is real but a design decision is needed before it can be coded at all

notes: Chapter-wide shared primitive; nearly every other candidate in this file depends on it, directly or as background context.
Brooks also gives an explicit boundary case: R21-... see RP4-02, a range that slopes too much is instead a trend channel.

candidates.name: TrendChannelVsTradingRangeSlopeFilter
candidates.quote: It can be mostly horizontal, which indicates that the bulls and bears are in balance, or it can be slightly sloping... If it slopes too much, it should be considered to be a trend channel and not a trading range.
candidates.description: A sloping range is still a trading range only while its containing lines' slope stays below some magnitude; beyond that it should be classified as a trend channel instead.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (regime classification)

complexity.reason: needs a trend-line slope computed from the range's boundary pivots, and the cutoff magnitude is not given numerically

candidates.name: StopRunReversalBar
candidates.quote: The market runs stops repeatedly, often with strong trend bars, but then reverses direction on the next bar. For example, the market will have two bear trend bars that fall below a strong swing low, but then the market reverses up on the next bar.
candidates.description: One or more strong trend bars break below (long case: below, mirrored for short) a recent swing low, then the very next bar reverses and closes back above that swing low -- a stop-run pattern common in trading ranges.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the reversal bar's high

complexity.reason: needs a tracked recent swing-low pivot, but the break/reverse test itself is a two-bar comparison

candidates.name: FewConsecutiveTrendBarsFilter
candidates.quote: There are many bull and bear trend bars but few instances where there are three or four consecutive bull trend bars or bear trend bars.
candidates.description: A trading-range clue: trend bars occur often, but runs of 3-4 or more consecutive same-direction trend bars are rare; a run at or beyond that length argues against the trading-range classification.
candidates.pseudocode:
consecutiveTrendBarCount = countConsecutiveTrendBars(direction = UP);
looksLikeTradingRange = consecutiveTrendBarCount < maxConsecutiveTrendBars;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (regime clue, one input to RP4-01)

complexity.reason: a running streak count of a per-bar trend-bar classification, similar in shape to the corpus's existing ConsecutiveUpBars counter

notes: Structurally similar to ConsecutiveUpBars but counts trend-bar classification (body dominates range) rather than close-above-open, and is used as a range/trend regime clue rather than a standalone entry.

candidates.name: BarOverlapFractionFilter
candidates.quote: Many bars overlap 50 percent or more of the bar before. There are many areas where there are three or more bars that each overlap by 50 percent or more of the range of the prior bars.
candidates.description: A trading-range clue: the current bar's range overlaps at least half of the prior bar's range; three or more such overlapping bars in a row strengthens the trading-range read.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (regime clue, one input to RP4-01)

complexity.reason: a bare comparison of the current bar's range against the prior bar's range

candidates.name: FlatMovingAverageFilter
candidates.quote: The moving average is relatively flat.
candidates.description: A trading-range clue: the moving average's slope over the last few bars is close to zero (neither clearly rising nor falling).
candidates.pseudocode:
maSlope = movingAverage[0] - movingAverage[maSlopeLookback];
isFlatMovingAverage = abs(maSlope) <= flatMaThreshold;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (regime clue, one input to RP4-01)

complexity.reason: an EMA plus a simple lagged-difference slope test; the flatness cutoff has no stated numeric value

candidates.name: FailedSpikeBreakoutVacuumReversal
candidates.quote: The vacuum effect is present, resulting in strong bull spikes at the top and strong bear spikes at the bottom, with both failing to break out and instead reversing back into the range.
candidates.description: Within an established trading range, a strong spike (one or more large trend bars) beyond the range's top or bottom fails to hold and reverses back inside the range within a few bars -- a failed-breakout entry back toward the opposite side of the range.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the reversal bar's low

complexity.reason: requires the trading-range context primitive plus tracked range boundaries and a recent-breakout/failure test

candidates.name: TradingRangeSetupLocationFilter
candidates.quote: When there is a bull trend, traders will buy a high 2 near the top of a leg, but when there is a trading range, they will buy a high 2 only if it is at the bottom of the range. Similarly, bears will short a low 2 at the bottom of a bear trend but they will short a low 2 in a trading range only when it is at the top of the range.
candidates.description: Inside a trading range, a High1/High2 buy setup is only valid near the BOTTOM of the range (not the top), and a Low1/Low2 short setup is only valid near the TOP of the range (not the bottom) -- the opposite of how those setups are traded in a trend. Setups at the 'wrong' extreme (High1/High2 near the top, Low1/Low2 near the bottom) usually fail and can be faded instead.
candidates.book_order_type: buy/sell stop per the underlying High1/High2/Low1/Low2 signal, gated by range location; the fade side uses a limit or stop-fade order at the opposite extreme

complexity.reason: composes the trading-range context and tracked range boundaries with existing pullback-count signal primitives (High1/High2/Low1/Low2), which this chapter assumes but does not itself define

notes: Restated multiple times in the chapter (pages 133, 137, 140-141) in different words -- this is one of the chapter's most repeated and distinctive ideas.

candidates.name: FinalLegChannelReversalBuySetup
candidates.quote: The final leg down in most trading ranges in bull markets is a bear channel, which is a last-ditch attempt by the bears to create a top and a new bear trend. A bear channel is a bull flag. Bulls can buy the reversal up from the bottom of the trading range or on the breakout pullback that usually follows soon afterward.
candidates.description: In a bull-trend trading range, the final leg down to the range's bottom is usually a channel (not a single spike); buy the reversal up from that bottom, or the breakout pullback that follows, since the channel down is functionally a bull flag.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the reversal bar's high

complexity.reason: needs the trading-range context, tracked range boundaries, and a spike-vs-channel classification of the final leg

candidates.name: SignalBarNotTooLargeNearRangeExtremeFilter
candidates.quote: Also, they should take the trade only if the signal bar is not too large, because they need to be entering near the extreme of the range and not in the middle.
candidates.description: A range-extreme reversal entry is only taken if its signal bar's range is not too large relative to recent bars -- an oversized signal bar would push the entry too far from the range's extreme and into its middle.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether a range-extreme reversal signal is acceptable)

complexity.reason: a window-average of bar range compared against the signal bar's own range

candidates.name: WaitForStopEntryReversalRatherThanFadeClose
candidates.quote: Only traders who are very experienced reading charts should fade the market on the close of breakout bars. Almost all traders are more likely to be successful if they wait to enter on a stop as the market reverses back into the range.
candidates.description: Rather than fading a breakout bar's close directly (an advanced, aggressive entry), wait for the market to reverse back into the range and enter on a stop as it does -- the safer, default form of a range-extreme reversal entry.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates which of two entry styles to use for a range-extreme reversal)

complexity.reason: the choice criterion is trader experience, not a bar-level test; for an automated system this collapses to always using the conservative stop-entry form

notes: For a mechanical system, this effectively means: always use the stop-entry-on-reversal form (RP4-03/RP4-07/R20-05 family), never the close-fade.

candidates.name: TradingRangeBreakoutStopBelowRangeLow
candidates.quote: a trader could buy the breakout on a stop and use a protective stop well below the bottom of the trading range... they need to place their protective stops far enough below the trading range so that the repeated failed downside breakouts will not stop them out.
candidates.description: For a with-trend buy on a trading-range's upside breakout, place the protective stop well below the bottom of the trading range (not just below the signal bar), to survive repeated failed downside breakout attempts before the eventual successful one.
candidates.pseudocode:
protectiveStopPrice = rangeLow - stopBufferBelowRangeLow;
exitLongOnStop = low[0] <= protectiveStopPrice;
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop order

complexity.reason: a fixed offset below a tracked range boundary; the range boundary itself is assumed already known/tracked

candidates.name: TradingRangeBreakoutEntryGatedByTrendResumption
candidates.quote: Sometimes a breakout above a trading range in a bull trend is a good entry on a buy stop, but only when the bull trend clearly has started to resume before the breakout.
candidates.description: Only take a trading-range's with-trend breakout entry when the larger trend has clearly already started to resume before the breakout occurs; otherwise prefer entering within the range as the trend resumes, or wait for a breakout pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the range high

complexity.reason: the gating condition ('trend clearly resuming') is exactly the always-in-direction design decision, not a stated bar-level test

candidates.name: TightRangeStopEntryAvoidance
candidates.quote: If the trading range is only three or sometimes even four points tall, entering on stops is usually a losing strategy. The trading range is then a relatively tight trading range... Most of the trades require limit order entries.
candidates.description: When the trading range's height is at or below a small threshold (the book's Emini example: 3-4 points), avoid stop-entry breakout/reversal trades; prefer limit-order entries instead.
candidates.pseudocode:
rangeHeight = rangeHigh - rangeLow;
avoidStopEntries = rangeHeight <= tightRangeHeightThreshold;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates stop-entry vs limit-entry style)

complexity.reason: needs tracked range boundaries; the threshold is instrument-specific (points, not ticks or ATR-normalized) as printed

notes: The book's threshold is in raw price points for the Emini specifically; an ATR- or tick-normalized version would generalize better across instruments.

candidates.name: MicroChannelSecondEntryFilter
candidates.quote: if you are looking to trade and the leg that is testing the top or bottom of the range is a tight channel, it is better to wait for a breakout pullback, which is a second entry... do not short below the low of the prior bar -- the upward momentum is too strong. Instead, wait to see if there is a pullback from this micro channel breakout.
candidates.description: When the leg testing the top or bottom of the range is itself a tight (micro) channel, do not take the naive fade against it; wait instead for a pullback from that micro-channel's eventual breakout (a second-entry setup).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether to fade the leg directly or wait for its breakout pullback)

complexity.reason: needs a micro-channel detector (small consistent-direction bar ranges with high overlap) applied to the leg testing the range extreme

candidates.name: RecentDirectionalPressureConfirmation
candidates.quote: Any short setup is also more reliable if there is other evidence of strong bears entering the market within the prior 10 bars, like two or three bars around this level with large tails on top, or several recent bars with strong bear bodies.
candidates.description: A range-extreme reversal setup is more reliable when, within the prior N bars, there is additional evidence of directional pressure at that level -- multiple bars with prominent tails on the relevant side, or multiple bars with strong same-direction bodies.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (confirmation filter, raises confidence rather than gating outright)

complexity.reason: counts of per-bar tail/body classifications over a window, each individually simple but combined into a multi-bar confirmation test

candidates.name: MiddleOfDayMiddleOfRangeCautionFilter
candidates.quote: The middle third of the day, from around 8:30 a.m. until 10:30 a.m. PST, can be difficult for traders on days that are not clearly trending... If the market is trading in the approximate middle of the day's range... and it is now in the middle of the day's trading hours, the chance of a tight trading range with overlapping bars, big tails, and multiple small reversals is significant.
candidates.description: During the middle third of the trading session (the book's example: 8:30-10:30 a.m. PST) while price sits near the middle of the day's range, expect choppy, low-quality price action; avoid anything less than a very good entry and prefer waiting for a test of the day's high or low.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter that raises the entry-quality bar rather than blocking entries outright)

complexity.reason: a time-of-day window test plus the day's running high/low and a proximity-to-midpoint test, each simple, combined into one filter

notes: The book explicitly frames the time window as a guideline, not a hard rule ("the time parameters are only guidelines... the overriding factor is the price action") -- see Figure PIV.4 discussion, page 142.

candidates.name: ClimaxImpliesTradingRangeTransition
candidates.quote: Whenever there is a spike up and then a spike down, or vice versa, the market has formed a climax reversal... This two-sided trading that usually takes place after a climax is a trading range, and it can be as brief as a single bar or can last for dozens of bars. The eventual breakout will usually lead to a measured move that approximates the height of the spike.
candidates.description: A sharp spike in one direction immediately followed by a sharp spike in the opposite direction (a buy or sell climax) is typically followed by a transition into a trading range, whose eventual breakout tends to approximate a measured move equal to the height of the initiating spike.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (regime-transition context flag)

complexity.reason: depends on spike/climax pattern recognition and a regime-transition judgment, both design decisions

candidates.name: ConsecutiveClimaxReversalOddsFilter
candidates.quote: Consecutive sell climaxes usually lead to a pullback, at least to the moving average, lasting at least 10 bars and having at least two legs, and sometimes they can lead to a trend reversal.
candidates.description: Two or more consecutive climaxes in the same direction raise the odds of at least a two-legged pullback lasting a minimum number of bars (toward the moving average), and increase the odds of an eventual trend reversal.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter raising expectation of a with-trend pullback / possible reversal)

complexity.reason: needs the underlying climax primitive plus a persistent streak counter across possibly non-adjacent climax bars

candidates.name: DoubleFailedBreakoutImpliesOppositeDirection
candidates.quote: When the market tries something twice and fails both times, it usually then tries the opposite.
candidates.description: After the market has attempted and failed to break out of a trading range in one direction at least twice, the odds favor it next attempting a breakout in the opposite direction.
candidates.pseudocode:
failedUpBreakoutCount = countFailedBreakoutAttempts(direction = UP, lookback = attemptLookback);
expectOppositeBreakoutAttempt = failedUpBreakoutCount >= minFailedAttempts;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter biasing the next expected breakout direction)

complexity.reason: needs a tracked count of recent failed-breakout attempts in one direction, itself dependent on a failed-breakout primitive

candidates.name: EndOfDayRangeReversalFilter
candidates.quote: the market often tries to reverse the final trading range in the last hour or so, so if the day is a bear trending trading range day, look for a buy setup at the low of the day going into the final hour or two of the day.
candidates.description: In a trending trading range day, the market often attempts to reverse the day's final trading range in the last one to two hours of the session; look for a counter-to-the-day's-trend setup at the day's extreme heading into the close.
candidates.pseudocode:
isFinalHoursOfSession = time[0] >= (sessionEndTime - finalReversalWindowMinutes);
lookForReversalAtDayExtreme = isFinalHoursOfSession && close[0] <= dayLow + dayExtremeTolerance;
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the reversal signal bar's high

complexity.reason: a time-window test plus proximity to the day's running extreme; the underlying 'trending trading range day' classification is itself a design decision

candidates.name: TrailingStopBelowRecentSwingLow
candidates.quote: As the trend progressed to new highs, they could have trailed their stops to below the most recent swing low. For example, after the market rallied above bar 11, their stops would then have been below bar 12, and they would have been protecting about nine points of profit.
candidates.description: As a with-trend rally progresses, trail the protective stop to just below the most recently formed swing low (mirrored: above the most recent swing high in a downtrend), tightening protection as new swing lows/highs form.
candidates.book_order_type: trailing protective stop order, moved up each time a new swing low forms

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection plus a persistent trailing-stop state that only ever moves in the favorable direction

candidates.name: StopBelowPriorBarLowForSpikeEntry
candidates.quote: If the SPY traders bought at the close of that second bull trend bar, they would have put their stops below the low of the first bull trend bar (one bar earlier), and their risk would have been about 12 points.
candidates.description: For an entry taken during a strong spike (e.g., buying the close of the spike's second bar), place the initial protective stop below the low of the bar immediately preceding the entry bar.
candidates.pseudocode:
initialStopPrice = low[1] - stopBuffer;
exitLongOnStop = low[0] <= initialStopPrice;
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop order placed at entry

complexity.reason: a fixed offset from the immediately prior bar's low

candidates.name: AlwaysInFlipEntry
candidates.quote: As a general rule, as soon as traders decide that there is now a bull trend underway, they should buy at least a small position at the market or on a tiny pullback... because the directional probability of an equidistant move is probably at least 60 percent.
candidates.description: As soon as the always-in direction is judged to have flipped to long, buy at least a small position immediately (at market, or on a minor pullback) rather than waiting for a full pullback entry, since the directional probability of an equidistant move is judged to be materially above 50%.
candidates.book_order_type: market order, or a limit order on a minor (sub-bar or lower-timeframe) pullback

complexity.reason: "always-in direction" is the MINING.md canonical research-grade example -- a design decision is needed before the flip itself can be detected at all

candidates.name: SpikeHeightMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: Traders measured the height from the bar 9 bottom to the bar 11 top of the bull spike and added that to the top of the bar 11 spike.
candidates.description: After a spike (a fast, mostly one-directional leg), project a measured-move target equal to the spike's own height (its start extreme to its end extreme), added from the spike's ending extreme.
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit (or discretionary scale-out) at the measured-move price

complexity.reason: the spike's start/end extremes require pivot/leg identification; the projection arithmetic itself is trivial

notes: Same measured-move family as R18-07/R18-08 (chapter 18) and R20-07 (chapter 20); this chapter repeats the idea for spikes specifically (see also RP4-18's climax-spike measured move). The dedup pass should merge all of these into one generic measured-move primitive family.

rejected.quote: If the market does not race to your profit target within seconds, the chances are high that you have been trapped. In this case, it is almost always better to place a limit order to get out at breakeven.
rejected.reason: requires sub-bar / tick-level timing ('within seconds') that the engine cannot observe from OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: Your personal radar can tell you if the market is more likely in a trend instead of a strong leg within a trading range. If you have a sense of uncertainty, the market is more likely in a trading range; if instead you have a sense of urgency...
rejected.reason: pure discretion (a trader's felt sense of uncertainty/urgency), no bar-level test

rejected.quote: If the trend was very strong, then the directional probability in the middle of the range might be 53 to 55 percent, although it is impossible to ever be certain.
rejected.reason: a probabilistic narrative the text itself calls unknowable ('impossible to ever be certain'), with no fixed bar-level test -- offered as color for RP4-01/RP4-13, not a standalone candidate

chapter_summary: This long Part IV introduction defines the trading range as any area of two-sided trading (a 'research'-grade concept per MINING.md's own example) and spends most of its length on trader psychology, probability narrative, and nine worked chart examples (Figures PIV.1-PIV.9) illustrating the same handful of recurring ideas: ranges are continuation patterns whose breakouts mostly fail (~80%); the classic pullback-setups (High1/High2, Low1/Low2) only work at the OPPOSITE range extreme from where they work in a trend; the final leg of a range is usually a channel (a with-trend flag) rather than a spike; climaxes and consecutive climaxes push the market into (and eventually out of) trading ranges; and several concrete tactical filters (signal-bar size, tight-range stop avoidance, micro-channel second entries, time-of-day caution, trailing/initial stop placement). Many statements are restated 3-4 times across different chart examples in different words; candidates above consolidate each distinct mechanizable idea once. Several candidates (RP4-01 TradingRangeContext, RP4-18 climax-to-range transition, RP4-24 always-in flip) are exactly the MINING.md-cited 'research' grade examples and should be treated as chapter-wide dependencies for the rest of the trading-range material still to be mined (Chapter 22 and beyond).
